You will find a lot of bullshit about "positive law" on the Internet. The term has been abused (maybe intentionally, maybe innocently).

Here is the truth:

All statutes passed by Congress are complied into the Statues at Large, starting from the first statute passed by Congress in 1789.

https://www.loc.gov/law/help/statutes-at-large/index.php

Over many years, it became difficult to find a law that was written, say 72 years ago, because the Statutes at Large are all in chronological order. It's damn near impossible to figure out what any law is on any particular subject by using only the Statutes at Large, especially when you also have to track down any number of amendments that came later, and in some cases a statute from a long time ago was completely repealed. How do you find it all? In the first 10-20 years or so, it was not a big deal. But over time, it became a tangled mess, and difficult to find anything on any particular subject.

So, about 50-100 years or so in, they decided to create the United States Code, which is more of an index style, and makes it easier to look things up by subject matter (rather than chronological date of enactment).

The problem was this: How do we know that the people responsible for copying the actual statutes from the Statues at Large over to the US code were writing the exact same language into the US Code (including everything, not omitting anything), especially when many of the statutes had been amended and re-amended?

So over time, Congress has established committees to review many of the titles in the US Code to verify that they are exactly the same as the statutes that were passed by Congress and published in the Statutes at Large.

About half of the titles have been verified as accurate, and those are called "positive law." The others have not.

Positive law can be cited in court and is considered accurate as to what the statutes actually say. Non-positive law is still cited, but can be refuted if you can find that the actual statutes say something different.

At this point, in the 21st century, I suspect they will not do anymore positive law analysis. The reason is that Title 26 (internal revenue) is not positive law, and will never be positive law because it has so much fraud intertwined into it. It would become too obvious if the only title not declared as positive law was the income tax. So, they will just leave it as is.

Here is a list of the titles and which are, and are not, positive law:

https://www.llsdc.org/assets/sourcebook/usc-pos-law-titles.pdf

Other things you read on the Internet about what "positive law" is, and that are in disagreement with what I wrote, are either unintentional misinformation or intentional disinformation.
